newsitem.title: MOROCCO: Morocco to keep tariff control on cereals imports.
newsitem.headline: Morocco to keep tariff control on cereals imports.

text.p: Morocco, which launched a gradual commodity liberalisation last year, will maintain tariffs over cereals imports this year to protect farmers and local industry, Agriculture Minister Hassan Abou Ayoub said on Wednesday.
He told a news conference "Cereals imports and exports are free but the state will ensure a protection (tariffs) at Morocco's borders to boost sale flow of domestic production at lucrative prices."
Earlier this year the government imposed new customs duties on soft wheat imports equivalent to $34 per tonne.
The tax took effect on January 25, 1997 and would remain in place until further notice, officials said.
Morocco was expected to import between 2.4 and 2.5 million tonnes of soft wheat in the 1997/98 season, up from 1.1 million tonnes in 1996/97, Abou Ayoub said.
"We will face a serious problem to co-ordinate logistics of cereals imports through the country's ports, including the Casablanca harbour," he said.
Morocco's has 11 ports, most of them located on the Atlantic coast.
The minister said the authorities had set a price for domestic soft wheat purchases of 2,500 dirhams ($266) per tonne and a premium for stockpiling of 20 dirhams per tonne.
The average price of imported soft wheat was between 2,300 and 2,600 dirhams per tonne in 1996/97.

Imports of other commodities such as vegetable oil and raw sugar are free but subject to varying tariffs. The state-owned Caisse de Compensation fund subsidises sales of these products at between 2,000 and 5,000 dirhams per tonne, a market analyst said.
